title: Nitrogen-fixing partnerships for major cereal crops

concept.text: The innovation would enable major cereals such as rice, wheat or maize to obtain agronomically meaningful amounts of nitrogen from atmospheric nitrogen through a regulated partnership with nitrogen-fixing microbes. The crop would recognize and accommodate suitable partners, support their nitrogen-fixing activity and receive nitrogen in a form it can assimilate. The ambitious target is reliable provision of most crop nitrogen through this partnership.

Established nitrogen-fixing symbioses provide a biological model for this capability. Microbial nitrogenase converts atmospheric nitrogen into reduced nitrogen, and symbiotic bacteroids export fixed nitrogen primarily as ammonia for plant assimilation into amino acids. The host supplies carbon and helps maintain conditions compatible with fixation. Extending this coordinated exchange to major cereals would require integration of recognition, microbial accommodation, oxygen management, nutrient transfer and regulation.

Scope synthesis. The concept permits different physical arrangements and signaling routes that achieve controlled, sustained nitrogen delivery. A legume-like root nodule is one possible architectural model. Other arrangements could qualify if they provide the necessary microbial habitat, reciprocal exchange and host regulation under agricultural conditions.

significance.text: Reliable majority-nitrogen provision would extend to major cereals a capability associated with nitrogen-fixing symbioses in certain other plant lineages. Its revolutionary significance would come from making atmospheric nitrogen a dependable source of crop nutrition through a functioning biological partnership. This is a conditional assessment of the proposed capability, with success dependent on completing the linked biological and agricultural requirements.

The direct agricultural opportunity would be displacement of a substantial share of applied nitrogen fertilizer while maintaining useful crop production. Lower fertilizer demand could reduce dependence on purchased nitrogen inputs. The extent of displacement would depend on how much fixed nitrogen actually reaches the crop, when it becomes available and whether the partnership performs consistently across soils and seasons.

Impact synthesis. Lower net emissions, reduced nitrogen losses to water and improved farm economics are conditional downstream possibilities. Their assessment requires complete nitrogen accounting, measured fertilizer displacement, yield comparisons and the costs of establishing and maintaining the partnership. Nitrogen fixation requires host carbon and microbial energy, so agricultural value also depends on the balance between nitrogen supplied and resources consumed. The analogy with established symbiotic crops supplies a functional model whose transferability to cereal production remains to be demonstrated.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is an integrated cereal–microbe partnership that transfers enough atmospheric nitrogen to support the crop reliably under variable field conditions. Recognition must connect to appropriate accommodation, sustained microbial activity, nutrient exchange and coordinated host development. The supplied review describes these linked functions in established symbioses and identifies environmental dependence and inconsistent field performance as obstacles to agricultural microbiome engineering.

Oxygen management creates a concrete engineering challenge. Effective fixation requires stable microaerobic conditions, intact nitrogenase and sufficient energy and electron supply. A successful partnership must protect the fixation machinery while sustaining the metabolism of both partners. Host carbon provision and microbial nitrogen export must remain coordinated so that fixation produces a useful nutritional return for the crop.

Signal perception is an early component of a larger developmental program. The retained review describes receptor-mediated symbiotic signaling, calcium signaling and downstream regulation in established plant–microbe associations. Connecting such signals to a complete cereal partnership would require coordinated cellular and developmental responses. Specific claims about remaining transcriptional barriers in engineered rice await access to the cereal-engineering discussion cited by the research.

Robust deployment also requires effective colonization and sustained exchange across different soils and environmental conditions. The review identifies inconsistent microbial-inoculant performance in the field as a bottleneck. An engineered partnership would therefore need both biological integration within the host and reproducible function in the surrounding agricultural environment.

current_state.text: The supplied 2026 review by Wei and colleagues, The plant microbiome: From ecological foundations to precision microbial engineering for sustainable agriculture, describes the biological basis of established nitrogen-fixing symbioses. Its retained text covers recognition, accommodation, oxygen protection, host carbon supply, nitrogen export and coordinated regulation. It also describes restricted phylogenetic distribution of root-nodule symbiosis. These observations ground the proposed cereal capability and its integration challenges.

The retained review also describes general symbiotic calcium signaling, including decoding of calcium spiking by CCaMK/DMI3 and phosphorylation of IPD3. This supports a mechanistic account of signaling in established symbioses. Its evidentiary scope here is general symbiotic biology, with cereal-specific engineering outcomes requiring the relevant experimental material.

The reconciled research reports engineered rice receptors responding to rhizobial signals, including downstream calcium signaling, and cites a cereal-engineering subsection of the 2026 review. The supplied review assessment establishes that the retained XML ends before that discussion. Consequently, the rice receptor responses and associated claims about transcriptional barriers remain research leads whose experimental details are unresolved in this record. A signaling response would establish one component of a partnership, with majority-nitrogen provision requiring additional functional evidence.

The research also identifies a rice study attributed to Singh, Mandal and Reddy and associates it with DOI 10.1007/s11033-025-10851-2. The retained response from the supplied PubMed URL contains only a cookie challenge. The study's identity, authorship, date, methods and findings therefore remain unverified through that artifact. The access failure leaves the reported study unresolved and supplies no scientific evidence against its findings.

The available evidence has two important access boundaries. The saved review extraction contains 120,000 characters and is explicitly truncated, while the saved PubMed response contains 153 characters of access-challenge content. The supplied review assessment reports no inspected figure image and an empty search record. As a result, the latest state as of November 1, 2026 remains unestablished. The supplied material provides no verified quantitative demonstration of majority-nitrogen provision in a major cereal.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Independently reproduce multi-season field trials in at least two major cereals across varied soils. The trials should show that atmospheric nitrogen supplies most crop nitrogen while supporting useful yields. The two-cereal threshold and majority-nitrogen target are proposed evaluation choices for this concept. A finite trial program would establish the breadth of performance demonstrated within its tested crops, soils, seasons and management conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Two cereals achieve useful yields with majority atmospheric nitrogen

completion_criteria.text: Proposed attribution and accounting. Combine isotope tracing with complete nitrogen budgets to quantify atmospheric nitrogen entering the crop and distinguish contributions from soil nitrogen and fertilizer. Define the crop-nitrogen denominator, sampling period, accounting boundaries and uncertainty before interpreting a majority-nitrogen result. Measurements should connect fixation to nitrogen assimilation by the host and to crop performance.
completion_criteria.label: Isotope tracing and complete nitrogen budgets quantify atmospheric nitrogen assimilation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical comparisons. Compare yield, fertilizer inputs, nitrogen losses, emissions and costs against appropriate controls, including conventional production under comparable conditions and controls that isolate the partnership's contribution. Record how the partnership is established and maintained, along with its performance across seasons. These comparisons should identify the conditions under which biological nitrogen supply produces a practical benefit and the conditions under which performance deteriorates.
completion_criteria.label: Controlled comparisons establish conditions for practical benefits from nitrogen partnerships

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries. Independent teams should reproduce the central nitrogen-transfer and agronomic findings using sufficiently documented crop material, microbial partners and management methods. Reports should specify tested genotypes, soils, environmental conditions and failure cases. The review's account of inconsistent field performance motivates this emphasis on replication and environmental scope.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce nitrogen-transfer and agronomic findings with documented boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. BOT-16, Predictable control of plant–mycorrhizal nutrient exchange, has the closest functional overlap through microbial recognition, accommodation, reciprocal nutrient supply and host regulation. BOT-01 specifically requires atmospheric nitrogen fixation and delivery to cereals. BOT-16 concerns control of mycorrhizal exchange, whose nutrient sources and microbial physiology require their own treatment.

Roster-based synthesis. BOT-02, A functional carbon-concentrating photosynthetic system in rice, shares the challenge of integrating a complex biological capability into a major cereal. It addresses photosynthetic carbon acquisition. BOT-10, Plants that reliably deposit durable additional carbon in soil, and BOT-15, Broadly transferable perennial grain production, overlap through possible changes to crop resource allocation and agricultural environmental outcomes. Each retains a separate functional endpoint and requires its own performance evidence.

Roster-based synthesis. BOT-03, Whole-plant synthetic genome construction and rewriting, and BOT-04, An inexpensive, broadly transferable method to edit and regenerate plants, could provide enabling engineering capabilities. BOT-05, Predictive plant biology from genome to whole-organism performance, could help anticipate the consequences of introducing a resource-demanding symbiosis. Their success would support development of BOT-01, while nitrogen delivery through a functioning partnership remains a distinct demonstration.

Roster-based synthesis. BOT-08, Programmable, durable plant immunity against diverse pathogens, overlaps through host recognition and regulation of microbial interactions. BOT-12, A causal map of plant-wide communication and plasmodesmatal control, and BOT-17, Predictive control of plant cell-division planes and tissue patterning, overlap with signaling and developmental coordination that could support accommodation structures. BOT-14, Programmable, multigenerational epigenetic inheritance of adaptive plant traits, could become relevant if stable inherited regulation is used in a cereal partnership. These connections identify possible enabling knowledge while preserving each roster entry's independent objective.

unresolved_issues: The engineered rice receptor experiments, their dates, methods, response measurements and scope require verification from the cited cereal-engineering discussion or underlying primary studies.
The specific transcriptional barriers attributed to cereal engineering remain unresolved because the relevant review subsection is absent from the retained extraction.
The identity and findings of the rice study attributed to Singh, Mandal and Reddy, including its associated DOI and publication date, remain unverified through the supplied PubMed artifact.
The latest state as of November 1, 2026 cannot be established from the empty supplied search record and partially accessible sources.
A future evaluation protocol must define the crop-nitrogen denominator, accounting period, nitrogen-budget boundaries, uncertainty treatment and appropriate controls.

The supplied evidence does not determine which partnership architecture would achieve robust cereal nitrogen provision or quantify achievable fertilizer displacement, net environmental benefits and farm costs.

brief.title: Cereal crops fed by nitrogen from the air
possible: Farmers could grow rice, wheat or maize that gets most of its nitrogen from the air through a partnership with microbes, tiny organisms living with the crop. The plant would support suitable partners and receive nitrogen in a form it can use.
why: This could replace a substantial share of nitrogen fertilizer while maintaining useful harvests. Farmers could depend less on purchased inputs, with potential gains from lower costs, fewer emissions and less nitrogen entering water.

sources.showed: Their review describes how plants and microbes form partnerships that turn nitrogen from the air into plant nutrition. It explains how plants recognize partners, support them and coordinate nutrient exchange.
sources.cited_for: Established partnerships provide a biological model for supplying cereals with nitrogen from the air.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a cereal partnership that reliably supplies most crop nitrogen.

sources.who: Anjulata Singh, Pranab Kumar Mandal and Pallavolu Maheswara Reddy
sources.showed: They engineered rice with genes involved in recognizing bacterial signals. Bacteria colonized its root surface, and the transferred genes became more active after bacterial treatment.
sources.quote: Root hair deformation was also observed when transgenic rice roots were treated with purified SmNod Factor (SmNF), and the presence of nitrogen in the medium reduced the root hair deformation percentage.
sources.cited_for: Engineered rice can respond to signals used in established nitrogen-supplying partnerships.
sources.not_established: These responses do not establish nitrogen transfer to rice or a partnership that supports crop yields.

shown: In one team's experiments, engineered rice responded to bacterial signals by changing the shape of root hairs, fine extensions of root cells. This demonstrates an early step in recognizing a partner. Supplying most of a cereal crop's nitrogen through a sustained partnership remains a goal.
missing: Cereals still need to connect partner recognition to a lasting microbial home and coordinated nitrogen delivery.
The partnership must protect nitrogen fixation, the conversion of airborne nitrogen into usable nutrients, while meeting both partners' energy needs.
Enough nitrogen must reach the crop at the right time to support useful yields across soils and seasons.

milestones.label: Two cereals yield well with most nitrogen from air
milestones.explanation: Independent field trials would have to reproduce useful yields with most crop nitrogen coming from air in at least two major cereals across varied soils and seasons. This would establish the demonstrated range of performance.

milestones.label: Tracing measures the nitrogen reaching the crop
milestones.explanation: Isotope tracing, which tracks distinguishable forms of nitrogen, and complete nitrogen budgets would have to quantify the crop's airborne supply. This would establish its share alongside soil and fertilizer contributions.

milestones.label: Controlled comparisons establish practical benefits
milestones.explanation: Controlled comparisons would have to measure yields, fertilizer use, nitrogen losses, emissions and costs, including partnership upkeep. This would identify where the partnership provides practical benefits and where performance deteriorates.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce nitrogen delivery and crop performance
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce nitrogen transfer and crop performance with documented plants, microbes, methods, environments and failures. This would establish reproducibility and the boundaries of success.

uncertain: Which physical arrangement can sustain a regulated cereal–microbe partnership under field conditions remains open.
The share of crop nitrogen supplied from air depends on how the crop total, measurement period and accounting boundaries are defined.
The balance between nitrogen delivered and plant resources consumed will determine achievable fertilizer savings and farm benefits.

page.title: Host-regulated nitrogen-fixing symbioses in cereals
page.definition: A cereal obtains most of its nitrogen from atmospheric nitrogen through a microbial partnership controlled by the host plant. The microbes convert nitrogen gas into ammonia, supply nitrogen to the cereal and receive plant carbon.

goal.need: About 70% of ammonia is used for fertilisers, according to the IEA’s 2021 assessment. Its production consumes energy and releases carbon dioxide at the quantities shown below. Nitrogen-fixing cereal partnerships address agricultural demand for this industrial nitrogen source.

figures.caption: Ammonia production in the IEA’s 2021 assessment
rows: 8.6 EJ, approximately 2% of global final energy consumption
figures.note: Both quantities cover total ammonia production.

statements.quote: ENSA scientists are investigating how to transfer nitrogen-fixing symbiosis of legumes into cassava and maize, two of the world’s most important crops.

statements.body: US National Science Foundation and UK Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council
statements.quote: reduce inputs of nitrogen fertilizers to non-leguminous crops whilst maintaining or increasing yield.
statements.context: The joint Nitrogen: Improving on Nature solicitation identifies this as its research objective.

statements.quote: fix more than 50% to 75% of their total nitrogen requirement.
statements.context: Philip Poole’s commissioned aspiration paper discusses this nitrogen-supply level across nitrogenase-transfer, nodulation and rhizosphere-engineering approaches.

completion.title: A cereal obtains most of its nitrogen through a host-regulated microbial partnership in the field.
completion.criterion: For one cereal, a host-regulated microbial partnership supplies more than 50% of the nitrogen accumulated by the whole crop between sowing and grain maturity under field conditions, while grain yield is maintained with reduced nitrogen fertiliser. Isotope-based measurements attribute nitrogen to the partnership, with matched non-fixing controls and accounting for seed, soil, fertiliser and deposition nitrogen. Independent field experiments reproduce the combined nitrogen-supply and yield result.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational definition combining published nitrogen-supply aspirations, host-control demonstrations and agronomic objectives.
completion.basis: Searches of ENSA objectives, NSF–BBSRC solicitation 12-579, the UK foresight report and published fixation-assessment criteria found no operational test combining majority nitrogen supply, host regulation and maintained field yield. Atlas defines majority as more than 50%, using the lower boundary of the report’s 50–75% discussion, and adds the programme’s yield objective and published independent-verification criteria.

milestones.title: A cereal root recognises rhizobial Nod factors and activates symbiosis responses.
milestones.criterion: A cereal root recognises Nod factors, bacterial signals that activate symbiosis responses. The BBSRC target is recognition of rhizobial bacteria. Rice carrying five legume genes showed Nod-factor-induced root-hair deformation in the study published on 22 July 2025. A related study published on 29 July 2025 reported root-hair calcium fluxes and nuclear calcium spiking. Sample sizes are unavailable in the accessible abstracts.
milestones.set_by: BBSRC award BB/K003712/1, Technical Summary, for the rhizobial engineering route.
milestones.threshold_quote: engineer cereals for recognition of rhizobial bacteria

milestones.title: A cereal controls nitrogenase activity in bacteria associated with its roots.
milestones.criterion: Plant-produced signals control nitrogenase, the microbial nitrogen-fixing enzyme, in root-associated bacteria. Haskett and colleagues demonstrated this in rhizopine-producing barley on 11 April 2022. At nine days after inoculation, activity was assayed after 48 hours at 1% oxygen. The T2 barley line supported 3.63 nmol ethylene h−1 plant−1 in the acetylene-reduction assay, approximately 5% of wild-type bacterial activity. Root imaging sampled five plants per treatment.
milestones.set_by: Synthetic-symbiosis experimental practice, represented by Haskett and colleagues’ published host-specific nitrogenase proof of concept, developed in barley.
milestones.threshold_quote: activation was specific to RhiP barley

milestones.title: A cereal incorporates nitrogen fixed by its microbial partner into its own organic compounds.
milestones.criterion: Nitrogen supplied as purified 15N2 gas enters the cereal’s own organic compounds. ACIAR describes plant 15N enrichment as direct proof of fixation. A maize study published on 12 November 2024 traced 15N into shoot chlorophyll across three experiments with six or seven plants per treatment. Wheat root enrichment was reported on 6 August 2025 with n = 8, with residual root-associated bacterial nitrogen identified as a possible contributor.
milestones.set_by: ACIAR Monograph 136, section 10.2.1, describing the field’s direct isotope-incorporation test for associative nitrogen fixation.
milestones.threshold_quote: Enrichment of the plant with 15N provides unequivocal proof

milestones.title: A field-grown cereal accumulates statistically detectable nitrogen from associated fixation.
milestones.criterion: Field-grown cereals accumulate nitrogen attributable to associated fixation, with statistically significant isotope differences from suitable non-fixing references. ACIAR specifies this outcome for associative fixation. Sierra Mixe maize experiments in three fields during 2016 and 2017 used five replicate blocks and estimated 31–55% nitrogen derived from the atmosphere by isotope dilution. Giller and colleagues subsequently challenged the choice and behaviour of reference plants in these experiments.
milestones.set_by: ACIAR Monograph 136, chapter 10, applying isotope-based fixation assessment to non-nodulating plants in non-sterile field soil.
milestones.threshold_quote: statistically significant inputs of fixed N to inoculated plants

milestones.title: A cereal partnership supplies the yield response of 25–50 kg fertiliser nitrogen per hectare.
milestones.criterion: Microbial nitrogen delivery produces a crop response equivalent to applying 25–50 kg fertiliser N ha−1, with maintained or increased grain yield. A maize study published on 12 November 2024 reported 58 commercial-field comparisons during 2021 with 39–45 kg N ha−1 less fertiliser. Mean yields were 13.42 and 13.43 Mg ha−1 for inoculated reduced-N and conventional treatments, respectively, with p = 0.871. The study used side-by-side field areas and included Pivot Bio authors.
milestones.set_by: ENSA developers Rogers and Oldroyd’s published initial engineering target, combined with the NSF–BBSRC yield objective. The quantitative target was motivated by maize production in sub-Saharan Africa.
milestones.threshold_quote: provide levels of fixed nitrogen equivalent to 25–50 kg·ha−1.

not_found: No located study jointly demonstrated majority nitrogen supply, host regulation and maintained field grain yield under independent replication.
Full methods and sample sizes for the two July 2025 rice receptor studies were unavailable through the accessible publisher previews.

results.detail: Purified S. meliloti Nod factor induced root-hair deformation; nitrogen in the medium reduced the deformation percentage.
results.quote: Root hair deformation was also observed when transgenic rice roots were treated with purified SmNod Factor (SmNF), and the presence of nitrogen in the medium reduced the root hair deformation percentage.

results.finding: Barley: 54 of 72 wild-type root cells showed calcium spiking in response to rhizobial Nod factor.
results.detail: Cells were exposed to 10⁻⁷ M S. meliloti LCO. The paper reports nutrient-dependent LCO recognition; the number of plants represented by the 72 cells is not specified in the table.

results.finding: Field-grown Sierra Mixe maize, in 3 fields with 5 replicate blocks, obtained an estimated 31%–55% of nitrogen from the atmosphere.
results.detail: Isotope differences were significant in 4 of 6 field experiments. The suitability and behavior of the reference plants were subsequently challenged.

results.finding: Field-grown maize at 16 sites: an estimated 11% of nitrogen was derived from the atmosphere.
results.detail: The high inoculation rate showed significant isotope dilution versus uninoculated maize, but the control was not established as non-fixing. The authors also note that greater fertilizer recovery could partly explain the isotope difference.
results.quote: These translated to 11% Ndfa across both treatments (95% CI: 0, 22%).

results.finding: Field-grown wheat, sample size not stated: inoculation with Bacillus C-11-25 yielded an estimated 23.9% atmospheric nitrogen in 1984.
results.detail: The field study used ¹⁵N isotope dilution, but the supplied text does not establish statistically significant isotope differences from suitable non-fixing references. It reports significant cultivar-by-inoculant interactions, which is a different result.

results.finding: Field-grown inoculated NIAB-6 rice, four replicates: 28.9% of plant nitrogen was estimated to derive from the atmosphere.
results.detail: The microplot experiment estimated fixation using 15N dilution and reported a significant increase in nitrogen fixed versus uninoculated rice. It did not report a statistical test of isotope differences against the purported non-fixing reference, whose fixation was assumed inhibited by a higher fertilizer dose.

results.finding: Rice inoculation in two pot and four field experiments produced a yield equivalent to 25–30 kg more fertiliser N.
results.detail: The strain was selected for its in vitro nitrogen-fixation potential, but the text does not establish that microbial nitrogen delivery caused the yield response.
results.quote: It was possible to evaluate the nitrogen fertilizer equivalent of inoculation (NFEI): at the medium rate of N fertilizer, inoculation ensured a yield equivalent to that obtained in the uninoculated control with 25 to 30 kg more nitrogen fertilizer.
